content.text: A
domain event
tells other parts of the same domain, in the same process, that something happened, and its handlers often run inside the same transaction, before the commit. An
integration event

tells other services, and must go out only after the commit, as a stable contract. Publishing a domain event straight to a broker gets the timing, the payload and the failure handling wrong; translate it into an integration event and stage it in an outbox instead.
The Ordering service raises
OrderPlaced

when an order is placed, and a handler already reserves stock for it. Shipping needs to know too, so someone adds a second handler that publishes the same event to the message broker. It works in every demo, until a customer double-clicks "Place order", the second save fails on a unique order number, and Shipping receives a message for an order that doesn't exist. A week later, a restart between a commit and a publish loses a message, and an order that does exist never ships.
The common misconception
The belief: domain events and integration events are the same thing, so a domain event can go straight to the message broker. An event is an event; why model it twice?

It's a reasonable reading of the sources. Microsoft's architecture guide says outright that, semantically, domain and integration events are the same thing: notifications about something that just happened. Both describe something that already happened and are named in the past tense, which matches Martin Fowler's description of a domain event as a record of something that happened. Vaughn Vernon, quoted in the same guide, suggests delivering domain events to asynchronous subscribers. But the guide follows that line with the one that matters: their implementation must be different.
What actually happens
Same fact, two audiences

A domain event is for the rest of your own domain. Microsoft's guide describes it as something you want other parts of the same domain, in-process, to be aware of, with handlers in the application layer that update other aggregates or start application actions. An integration event exists to propagate committed changes to other microservices, bounded contexts or external applications, and it always travels asynchronously, across processes, through an event bus. One is an internal call with a nicer shape. The other is a published API.
Domain events run before the commit; integration events must wait for it
The guide's reference app dispatches domain events right before
SaveChanges
, on purpose: handlers that use the same scoped
DbContext

add their changes to the same transaction, so the order and its side effects succeed or fail together. Integration events have the opposite rule. They should go out only if the entity was saved, otherwise it's as if the whole operation never happened.
A broker publish inside a domain event handler breaks that rule. In a test with EF Core 10 on SQLite, a handler published
OrderPlaced
to a fake broker, then
SaveChangesAsync
failed with
UNIQUE constraint failed: Orders.Number
. The broker held one message, and the order wasn't in the database.
After the commit isn't enough on its own
Moving the publish after
SaveChangesAsync

fixes that and opens the reverse gap: two writes, to the database and to the broker, with no transaction spanning both. The guide spells out the failure: if the service crashes after the database is updated but before the event is published, the system can become inconsistent. It advises against distributed transactions between the two and lists three ways out: full event sourcing, transaction log mining, or a
transactional outbox
table. In the test, a simulated crash between the commit and the publish left the order saved and the broker empty.
A domain event isn't a contract
Domain events may carry domain objects. The guide's own
OrderStartedDomainEvent
holds the
Order
entity, which is fine in-process. Put it on the wire and the entity's shape becomes your public API. In the test, serializing an event that carried an order with a back-reference from its lines threw
JsonException: A possible object cycle was detected

. Even without a cycle, renaming a domain property would break every consumer. Integration events are plain data-holding classes, and the guide recommends defining them per service rather than in a library shared across services.
The fix: translate at the boundary, stage in an outbox

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right

content.text: The staged row is just the contract's type name and JSON payload, saved by the same
SaveChangesAsync
as the order. In the test, a failing save left no outbox row behind, and a successful one stored the order and its message together. A background service then publishes what's pending:

That comment is the deal you accept. In the test, a relay that crashed after publishing and before marking the row sent the same message twice. An outbox gives you at-least-once delivery, so consumers must be idempotent: processing a message twice has to leave the same result as processing it once.

rows.text: Your own domain, in the same process
Usually right before the commit, in the same transaction
Plain, versioned data that consumers depend on
A method call; fails with the request
Through a broker, at least once
The domain model, free to change
A public contract, changed with care

blocks.title: Opinion: you might not need integration events yet

content.text: This is our view, not a rule from the guide. If every handler lives in one process and one database, domain events and a single transaction are simpler and stronger than anything a broker offers. Add integration events when something outside the process genuinely needs to know, and add the outbox with them.

blocks.title: Never publish to a broker before SaveChanges

content.text: A handler that runs before the commit can't know whether the commit will happen. Anything it sends outside the process, a message, an email or a webhook, can describe data that was rolled back.

blocks.title: Give every integration event an id

content.text: Put a unique id in each outbox message and let consumers record the ids they've processed. That's what Microsoft's guide suggests, so a redelivered message is recognized and skipped.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Find publishes in domain event handlers

content.text: Search for broker, email and HTTP calls in code that runs before
SaveChangesAsync
, including
SaveChanges
overrides and interceptors.
Create separate records with primitive fields and a version in the name, owned by the publishing service, and map domain events to them in explicit code.
Add an outbox table and insert integration events in the same
SaveChangesAsync
as the business change.
Publish pending rows from a background service, and have every consumer detect duplicates or apply changes that are safe to repeat.
Key takeaways

items.text: Domain and integration events describe the same kind of fact for different audiences, so they're implemented differently.
Domain events usually run before the commit, in the same transaction; integration events must leave only after it.
Publishing from a domain event handler can announce data that was rolled back, and publishing after the commit can lose the message.
An outbox row saved with the business change closes that gap, at the price of at-least-once delivery.
Treat integration events as versioned public contracts and make every consumer idempotent.
